nodes.name: Two data rules of the big data viewpoint
nodes.statement: Two data rules are believed. For one thing, the data does not lie. For other thing, we only need to guarantee that our conclusion is correct with very large probability rather than one in the era of big data [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].

nodes.name: Conjecture on the nature of channel information
nodes.statement: Based on these results, we put forward a conjecture that there is nature of channel information and no matter Shannon mutual information, Chernoff mutual information or other information measures, which are different measures of the same information quantity.
nodes.statement_short: Conjecture: a single underlying channel information quantity exists, and Shannon, Chernoff and other measures are just different measures of it.
conclusions: there is nature of channel information and no matter Shannon mutual information, Chernoff mutual information or other information measures, which are different measures of the same information quantity

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information
nodes.statement: The mutual information is a measure of the amount of information that one random variable contains about another variable. In fact, it describes the reduction in the uncertainty of one random variable if another one is known [\cite{Elements}]. According to [\cite{Elements}], the Shannon mutual information is defined as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $X,Y$ are two random variables with marginal probability mass functions $p(x)$ and $p(y)$ and joint probability mass function $p(x,y)$. It is noted that $I(X;Y)$ is the relative entropy (or Kullback-leibler distance) between the joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and the product distribution $p(x)p(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon mutual information $I_S(X,Y)$ is the relative entropy between the joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and the product of the marginals.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.genus: the relative entropy (or Kullback-leibler distance) between the joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and the product distribution $p(x)p(y)$

nodes.name: relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler distance)
nodes.statement: The relative entropy is given by [\cite{Elements}]: \begin{equation} D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: KL divergence $D(p\|q)$ as the $p$-weighted sum of log-likelihood ratios.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory

nodes.name: Chernoff information
nodes.statement: The Chernoff information is derived from the problem of classic hypothesis testing. Chernoff Information is the resulting error exponent when minimizing the overall probability of error [\cite{Elements}]. As defined in [\cite{Elements}], it is given by \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\alpha$ is real parameter with $0\leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff information is the optimal error exponent $-\min_{0\le\alpha\le1}\log\sum_x P_1^\alpha(x)P_2^{1-\alpha}(x)$ in binary hypothesis testing.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
nodes.genus: the resulting error exponent when minimizing the overall probability of error

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: With the aid of Chernoff information to describe the relationship between the two variables, a new mutual information is defined as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} In this paper, we call it Chernoff mutual information relative to Shannon mutual information.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff mutual information: the Chernoff information taken between the joint law $p(x,y)$ and the product law $p(x)p(y)$.

nodes.name: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information use different distribution distances
nodes.statement: In fact, both Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are to depict the inner relationship between two random variables. The difference is that they adopt different measures of the distance between two distributions. The relative entropy is adopted in Shannon mutual information and the R{\'{e}}nyi divergence is used in Chernoff mutual information [\cite{van2014renyi}].

nodes.name: channel capacity
nodes.statement: The mutual information between the input and output of a channel can be used to describe the transmittability of a channel. For example, the maximum mutual information is defined as the channel capacity for a discrete memoryless channel. Obviously, the mutual information is the measure of channel information.
nodes.section: 2 Channel Information Measures and ACE Algorithm Description
nodes.statement_short: Channel capacity is the maximum mutual information of a discrete memoryless channel.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory

nodes.name: binary symmetric channel (BSC)
nodes.statement: Consider the BSC, which is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelBSC}. It is a binary channel where the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$. The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $. It is argued in [\cite{Elements}] that it reflects common characteristics of the general channel with errors though it is the simplest model.
nodes.statement_short: Binary symmetric channel with input distribution $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$ and transmission error $\varepsilon$.
nodes.origin_citation: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
differentia: the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$
The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: The Shannon mutual information is given by: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^2 {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^2 {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr & = (1 - \varepsilon )\log {{1 - \varepsilon } \over {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon }} + \varepsilon \log {\varepsilon \over {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )}}. \cr \end{aligned} \end{equation} It can be seen as $I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y))$.
nodes.statement_short: Closed form of the BSC Shannon mutual information in terms of $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: While the Chernoff mutual information is given by: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ &=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log ( {(1 - \varepsilon )^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon } \right)^{1 - \alpha }} \\ &+ {\varepsilon ^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )} \right)^{1 - \alpha }} ) \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: BSC Chernoff mutual information as a minimization over $\alpha\in[0,1]$ of a log-sum of $\lambda,\varepsilon$ terms.

nodes.name: No explicit solution for the BSC Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, there is no explicit solution for Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}). As a result, it is arduous to analyze the Chernoff mutual information.\\ It is observed that the Shannon mutual information seems to be completely different from the Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: multiple symmetric channel (MSC)
nodes.statement: The MSC is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelMBSC}. The number of input symbol is $M$. The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$).The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$. The BSC is the special case of MSC for $M=2$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiple symmetric channel with $M$ inputs, input law $(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_M)$ and per-symbol error $\varepsilon/(M-1)$; the BSC is the case $M=2$.
differentia: The number of input symbol is $M$
The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$)
The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: Similarly, the Shannon mutual information is given by: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^M {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^M {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: MSC Shannon mutual information as the double sum over the $M$ input and output symbols.

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: The Chernoff mutual information is given by: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {{p(xy)}^\alpha (x){(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: MSC Chernoff mutual information as a minimization over $\alpha\in[0,1]$ of a log-sum of joint and product laws.

nodes.name: ACE setting: predictors, response and zero-mean transformations
nodes.statement: Assume random variables $X_1,X_2,\cdots ,X_p$ are predictors and $Y$ is response. Supposing $\phi _1(X_1),\phi _2(X_2),\cdots,\phi _p(X_p),\theta (Y)$ are arbitrary zero mean functions of the corresponding variables

nodes.name: ACE residual error $e^2$
nodes.statement: the residual error is \begin{equation} {e^2}\left( {\theta ,{\phi _1},\cdots,{\phi _p}} \right) = {{E\left\{ {{{\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right]}^2}} \right\}} \over {E\left[ {{\theta ^2}(Y)} \right]}} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalized mean-squared residual $e^2$ of the additive model $\theta(Y)\approx\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)$.

nodes.name: ACE Algorithm
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\ \STATE End Inner Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\ \STATE End Outer Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Alternating conditional expectation: repeatedly replace each $\phi_k$ by the conditional expectation of the current residual and renormalize $\theta$, until $e^2$ stops decreasing.

nodes.name: Initialize the transformations
nodes.statement: set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;
nodes.statement_short: Initialize $\theta$ as the normalized response and all $\phi_k$ to zero.

nodes.name: Outer iteration loop
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;
nodes.statement_short: Open the outer loop, running until $e^2$ stops decreasing.

nodes.name: Inner iteration loop
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;
nodes.statement_short: Open the inner loop, again controlled by the decrease of $e^2$.

nodes.name: Update each predictor transformation
nodes.statement: For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;
nodes.statement_short: For each $k$, replace $\phi_k$ by the conditional expectation of the residual given $X_k$.

nodes.name: Close the inner loop
nodes.statement: End Inner Iteration Loop;

nodes.name: Update the response transformation
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;
nodes.statement_short: Replace $\theta$ by the normalized conditional expectation of $\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)$ given $Y$.

nodes.name: Close the outer loop
nodes.statement: End Outer Iteration Loop;

nodes.name: Return the optimal transformations
nodes.statement: $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;
nodes.statement_short: Return the converged $\theta^*,\phi_1^*,\dots,\phi_p^*$ as the solution.

nodes.name: Channel information as a function of the channel parameters
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,X_2,\cdots,X_p$ be the channel parameters and $Y$ be measured value of channel information. The functional relation between them is: \begin{equation} Y = f({X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The measured channel information $Y$ is modelled as $Y=f(X_1,\dots,X_p)$ of the channel parameters.

nodes.name: Channel parameters and the functional relation are known
nodes.statement: It is supposed that ${X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}$ are known and independent. Moreover, the functional relation $f$ is also known since it is defined by human to describe the channel information.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition of the channel information
nodes.statement: As a result, one can get \begin{equation} \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta \end{equation} where $\delta$ is residual error.
nodes.statement_short: ACE output: $\theta(Y)=\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)+\delta$, separating the influence of each channel parameter.

nodes.name: Simulation Procedure
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$; \STATE Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information; \STATE Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm; \STATE Repeat above process till the required times. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Monte Carlo loop: draw channel parameters, evaluate the channel information measures, decompose them by ACE, and repeat.

nodes.name: Generate channel parameters
nodes.statement: Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$;
nodes.statement_short: Draw the random channel parameters.

nodes.name: Evaluate the channel information measures
nodes.statement: Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information;
nodes.statement_short: Compute the information measures for the drawn parameters.

nodes.name: Decompose by ACE
nodes.statement: Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm;
nodes.statement_short: Run ACE on the computed measures.

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: Repeat above process till the required times.
nodes.statement_short: Loop the whole draw-compute-ACE cycle.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition of the BSC channel information
nodes.statement: $20000$ observations geneated from the Eq.(\ref{BSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with two input parameters.
nodes.statement_short: 20000 BSC samples with $\lambda,\varepsilon$ drawn independently from $U(0,1)$, fed to ACE.

nodes.name: Quality of the ACE decomposition on the BSC
nodes.statement: The ACE algorithm is applied to this simulated data set and the results is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$. Furthermore, The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero. Clearly, both of them have shown that the ACE decomposition results are excellent.

nodes.name: Coincidence of the BSC ACE transformations for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: It is noted that function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition. As a result, in the range of the errors permitted, the $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ appears to be coincided with each other. $\phi_1(\lambda)$ is monotone decreasing function. The greater $\lambda$, the faster the decline in $\phi_1(\lambda)$. Furthermore, $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is symmetric around the line $\varepsilon = 0.5$ for the fact that the channel is symmetrical about $\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: In the BSC the curves $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ coincide for both measures; $\phi_1$ decreases and $\phi_2$ is symmetric about $\varepsilon=0.5$.

nodes.name: Shannon values are smaller than Chernoff values in the BSC
nodes.statement: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole variant trend is identical. $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition of the MSC channel information
nodes.statement: $60000$ observations generated from the Eq.(\ref{MSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{MSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with four input parameters.
nodes.statement_short: 60000 MSC samples in $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\varepsilon$ drawn independently on $(0,1)$, fed to ACE.

nodes.name: ACE validity confirmed on the MSC
nodes.statement: Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I} shows similar characteristics that in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small. On the other hand, the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$. These two points verify the validity of the ACE algorithm again.

nodes.name: Shape of the MSC ACE transformations
nodes.statement: It is obviously that the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures. It is worth noting that the minimum of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ occurs when $\varepsilon \approx 0.75$. The values of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is big when $\varepsilon$ is very close to $0$ or $1$. Moreover, $\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$ and $\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ are very similar. Their function curve is flat and close to zero when the independent variable (the probability of the input symbol) is less than $0.7$ . When the independent variable approaches to $1$, the values of them rapid decrease. In fact, it is reasonable because these input variables are equivalent for the channel.
nodes.statement_short: In the MSC all ACE curves nearly agree across measures: $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is minimal near $\varepsilon\approx0.75$ and the $\phi_i(\lambda_i)$ are flat then drop as $\lambda_i\to1$.

nodes.name: Shannon values are smaller than Chernoff values in the MSC
nodes.statement: As illustrated in Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, the result of Shannon mutual information is smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole varying trend is identical. $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is also close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.

nodes.name: Big data justification for the numerical ACE analysis
nodes.statement: When more narrowly examined, there are more interesting conclusions. In this section, we analyze these ACE simulated results from the viewpoint of big data. There are several nature behind it. First of all, the data does not lie. Naturally, the ACE results can provide much true and useful information for us. Furthermore, we always turn to numerical analysis when it is difficult to do theoretical analysis. The complicated equations of Shannon or Chernoff mutual information are arduous to do intuitive theory analysis, especially when they are multivariable, so it is quite appropriate to do numerical analysis by ACE algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Because the data does not lie and the closed forms resist theory, a numerical big-data analysis by ACE is the appropriate tool.

nodes.name: probably approximately correct (PAC) model
nodes.statement: In fact, the probably approximately correct (PAC) model is enough for us in most of time [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}]. In this model, one only need to construct algorithms which guarantee that it is correct with high probability (not necessarily one). This model is the foundation of Support Vector Machine (SVM) [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].
differentia: one only need to construct algorithms which guarantee that it is correct with high probability (not necessarily one)

nodes.name: ACE result as a composition $Y=\psi(\varphi(\mathbf{X}))$
nodes.statement: The ACE results is \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $Y$ is the channel information and ${\textbf{X}}$ is all the set of all the input channel parameters. The equation ($a$) holds because the residual error $\delta$ can be ignored.
nodes.statement_short: The channel information factorizes as $Y=\psi(\varphi(\mathbf{X}))$ with $\psi=\theta^{-1}$, since the residual $\delta$ is negligible.

nodes.name: Shannon's $\theta^{-1}$ is bigger than Chernoff's
nodes.statement: From the figures above, it is noted that $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information. For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$. The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same. From the Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I} to Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, it is also noted that the function $\theta(\cdot)$ is monotonic function. As mentioned above, the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend and the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information. Therefore, the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's. Actually, the facts extremely agree with the this corollary, which can well explain the phenomena in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC1 C and I}.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\theta$ is monotonic and Shannon's $\theta(Y)$ is always below Chernoff's, Shannon's $\theta^{-1}$ exceeds Chernoff's.
assumptions: the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend and the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information
conclusions: the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's

nodes.name: Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff
nodes.statement: In this sense, Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff. Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R{\'{e}}nyi divergence when $\alpha=1$. The channel information measures deduced from them look very different even for the channel as simple as BSC. However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity. For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information are two different metrics of one and the same channel information quantity.
assumptions: For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given
conclusions: they are different metrics of the same physical quantity
all of its state and properties will be determined
Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent

nodes.name: Kilometer and centimeter as two measures of length
nodes.statement: For example, the kilometer and centimeter are both measures of length, but they are used in different situations for convenience. Generally speaking, we do not adopt the centimeter to measure the distance between two cities. In contrast, we would like adopt it to measure the length of the steel rule. Their true values are identical when measuring the same things, even their numerical values are different. Similarly, the Shannon and Chernoff information are two metrics of the same quantity of information.
nodes.statement_short: Unit analogy: km and cm measure the same length in different situations, as Shannon and Chernoff measure the same information.

nodes.name: Channel parameters decide the nature of the channel
nodes.statement: Obviously, the ability to convey information of a channel is decided by input parameters. That is to say, the parameters represent the channel. As a result, we hold opinion that these channel parameters decide the nature of channel.
assumptions: the ability to convey information of a channel is decided by input parameters
conclusions: these channel parameters decide the nature of channel

nodes.name: nature of channel information $\varPsi$
nodes.statement: In this paper, we take $\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}}\right)$ as the nature of channel information and we get \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the $\varPsi$ is the nature of channel information. It is only decided by the channel parameters and it contains the core of the channel information.
nodes.statement_short: The nature of channel information is defined as $\varPsi=\varphi(\mathbf{X})$, the measure-independent inner quantity fixed by the channel parameters alone.
differentia: It is only decided by the channel parameters
it contains the core of the channel information

nodes.name: Any channel information measure as a function of $\varPsi$
nodes.statement: The other physical quantity about channel information is just the function of $\varPsi$, just as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information.
nodes.statement_short: Every measurement of channel information is an outer function $\mathrm{I}=\psi(\varPsi)$ of the common inner quantity.

nodes.name: Shannon and Chernoff measures as compound functions
nodes.statement: As far as Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are concerned, their only difference is the function $\psi(\cdot)$. They can be seen as a compound function. The inner is $\varPsi$ which is the function w.r.t. channel parameters and the outer is the function w.r.t. $\varPsi$. For different channel information measures, the inner is always the same but the outer is different.

nodes.name: Conjecture: any novel information measure ACE-decomposes as $\psi(\cdot)$
nodes.statement: There is a conjecture that if a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information, it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent. This rule can be used to judge the rationality of the new information measure. This conjecture also provides a way for us to propose a new information measure for the fact that we can construct that based on designing the function $\psi(\cdot)$. In fact, even if this guess is not right with probability one, the new one which conforms to the law is correct with large probability and we can easily find the relation between that and previous information measures, such as Shannon and Chernoff information.
nodes.statement_short: Conjecture: any newly proposed channel information measure will ACE-decompose into an outer function $\psi(\cdot)$ of the same inner nature, which yields a rationality test for new measures.
assumptions: if a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information
conclusions: it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent
